parts.note: a plain definition of the old style: issued or flowed forth from a source

explanation.walkthrough: Early Times puzzles mixed in plain definitions like this one; there is no wordplay to find.
explanation.definitionFit: To issue forth from a source, as light or a rumour does, is to come out of it.

parts.note: read not as the idiom for perfect health but literally as the noise a bell makes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound as a bell' means in perfect condition; here 'sound' is the noun, the noise a bell makes.
explanation.definitionFit: The chime of a pealing bell is imitated by this doubled echoic word.

clue.text: It wasn't Wilkie Collins that was anonymous (two words)

definitions.text: It wasn't Wilkie Collins that was anonymous

parts.words: It wasn't Wilkie Collins that was anonymous
parts.note: the novelist signed his books, but one of his novels has a title meaning nameless

explanation.surface: A remark that the Victorian novelist Wilkie Collins never wrote anonymously.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilkie Collins was a Victorian novelist (The Woman in White); the anonymous thing is the title of his novel, not the author.
explanation.definitionFit: A Wilkie Collins novel of 1862 bears this title, which literally means lacking a name, the sense of anonymous.

clue.text: Quite inappropriately they are found in Manchester lanes (two words)

definitions.text: Quite inappropriately they are found in Manchester lanes

indicators.note: the letters are put in an unsuitable order, so they are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Sea-going vessels would be oddly placed in the streets of an inland city.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: ships of the English Channel would be out of place in Manchester's lanes, and 'Quite inappropriately' rearranges MANCHESTER LANES.
explanation.definitionFit: Ferries crossing between England and France are vessels that are wholly out of place in an inland city's streets.

definitions.meaning: a Mongol people of central Asia
a shaggy or coarse cloth named after that people; the plural is taken for pieces of it

explanation.surface: Members of an Asian tribe dressed in cotton fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: A Mongol people living by the Caspian give their name to a coarse shaggy fabric.

definitions.meaning: magnesium sulphate taken as a purgative, named after a Surrey town
a racecourse in Surrey where the Derby is run

explanation.walkthrough: Epsom is a town in Surrey, England: Epsom salts come from its spring, and the Derby horse race is run on its course.
explanation.definitionFit: The Surrey town gives its name to a bath salt and has a famous racecourse.

parts.note: a word meaning to weep noisily is also the fat of a whale

explanation.definitionFit: To weep noisily is one sense of the word; the other is the thick fat layer of a whale.

clue.text: Should be successfully worked by those with a grasp of horticulture

definitions.text: Should be successfully worked by those with a grasp of horticulture

parts.words: Should be successfully worked by those with a grasp of horticulture
parts.note: a grasp is a hold, and a small farm is something worked by a grower

explanation.surface: Advice that a plot of land thrives under gardeners who know their business.
explanation.definitionFit: A smallholding is a piece of rented land worked by its tenant, and the word also means gripping, as a grasp does.

parts.note: read not as an oath but as a musician naming the Greek god of music as his own

explanation.definitionFit: The Greek deity of music and poetry would be a musician's own patron god.

clue.text: One of them took off Ben Battle's legs, " so he laid down his arms "

definitions.text: One of them took off Ben Battle's legs, " so he laid down his arms "

parts.words: One of them took off Ben Battle's legs, " so he laid down his arms "
parts.note: quotes Thomas Hood's comic ballad Faithless Nelly Gray, where a soldier loses his legs to artillery shot

explanation.surface: A line from a comic poem about a soldier maimed in battle.
explanation.walkthrough: In Thomas Hood's poem, 'a cannon-ball took off his legs, so he laid down his arms': 'arms' is both weapons and limbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Round iron shot fired from artillery is what removed the soldier's legs in Hood's ballad.

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Ball mid (6)', has no definition: ORB inside MID gives MORBID, but nothing defines the answer and no word signals the insertion, so the clue is cut short.
Clue as held, 'Puma in confusion,', is cut short; the full PANDEMONIUM clue appears on 1-across instead, so it is shown on two lights.

parts.note: a pulse eaten by vegetarians is also old slang for a chap

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old bean' is a dated British form of address for a man, like 'old chap'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pulse is vegetarian fare, and 'old bean' is dated British slang for a fellow.

parts.note: the offer in the saying about paying for someone's thoughts is a small coin

explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'a penny for your thoughts' offers this coin in exchange for what someone is thinking.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying 'a penny for your thoughts' makes the small coin the price offered.

clue.text: "Tiger, tiger burning bright In the forests of the night" (——)

definitions.text: "Tiger, tiger burning bright In the forests of the night"

parts.words: "Tiger, tiger burning bright In the forests of the night"
parts.note: the opening lines of a famous poem, to be answered with the name of its poet

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the poet of the lines, William Blake, not anything in them.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the opening lines of The Tyger, by the English Romantic poet and engraver.

parts.note: an oak is a tree
an apple is a tree too

explanation.surface: A puzzle in which two trees produce a single fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: Two trees give OAK and APPLE; the oak apple is a gall, not a true fruit, which makes 'one fruit' a playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A gall growing on oak leaves and twigs looks like a small round fruit.

clue.text: Wicket-keepers should be good at: this game

definitions.text: Wicket-keepers should be good at: this game

parts.words: Wicket-keepers should be good at: this game
parts.note: a cricket keeper's job is to trap the ball, and that phrase names an old game

explanation.surface: A remark on what cricket keepers ought to excel at.
explanation.walkthrough: A wicket-keeper is the cricket fielder behind the stumps who catches the ball; trap-ball is an old game played with a wooden trap.
explanation.definitionFit: An old English bat-and-ball game uses a lever device that flicks the ball up, and catching a ball is what keepers do.

parts.note: a maiden is a miss and islands are isles, so run the two together

explanation.walkthrough: MISS (maiden) + ISLES (islands) makes the word; the clue gives no separate definition, only the punning split.
explanation.definitionFit: Projectiles thrown or fired at a target are named by a word that splits into a young woman's title and small islands.

clue.text: Evidently: there wasn't a skeleton in her cupboard

definitions.text: Evidently: there wasn't a skeleton in her cupboard

parts.words: Evidently: there wasn't a skeleton in her cupboard
parts.note: the nursery-rhyme old woman went to her cupboard and found it bare, without even a bone

explanation.surface: A woman with no shameful secrets hidden away.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'skeleton in the cupboard' is a hidden scandal; here it is read literally, since the rhyme's cupboard held no bone at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Mother Hubbard of the nursery rhyme found her cupboard bare, with not one bone in it.

clue.text: This saint is only sham and very sticky

definitions.text: This saint is only sham and very sticky

parts.words: This saint is only sham and very sticky
parts.note: a pretended saint is called a ... saint, and a sticking bandage has the same name

explanation.surface: A complaint about a fake holy figure who is also cloying.
explanation.definitionFit: A hypocrite is called a 'plaster saint', and an adhesive dressing for a cut shares the word.

parts.note: male deer said aloud sound like the red suit in a pack of cards

explanation.walkthrough: A pack of cards has a suit of hearts; the deer's name sounds the same, and 'pack' suggests hounds hunting deer.
explanation.definitionFit: Male red deer are called by a word that sounds like the card suit.

parts.note: Cowper's John Gilpin was a ...-band captain, so the word fills the gap before 'band'

explanation.surface: A statement about the citizen hero of Cowper's comic ballad.
explanation.walkthrough: In William Cowper's ballad John Gilpin is 'a citizen of credit and renown' and 'a train-band captain'; trainbands were London's citizen militia.
explanation.definitionFit: Cowper wrote that John Gilpin, a London citizen, was 'a train-band captain', a citizen militia.

parts.note: a plain definition: unpleasant to look at

explanation.walkthrough: A plain definition with no wordplay, as early Times puzzles sometimes gave.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unpleasant to look at is unattractive in appearance.

parts.note: concord points to a concordance of the Bible, compiled by one famous man

explanation.surface: A man who keeps peace on religious matters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concord' suggests harmony, but it stands for a concordance, an index of every word in the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexander Cruden compiled the standard concordance to the Bible in 1737.

clue.text: She's as headstrong as an allegory on the banks of the Nile

definitions.text: She's as headstrong as an allegory on the banks of the Nile

parts.words: She's as headstrong as an allegory on the banks of the Nile
parts.note: a famous misused-word line from Sheridan's The Rivals, alligator turned into allegory

explanation.surface: A line comparing a stubborn woman to a creature of the Nile.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is itself an example: Mrs Malaprop's line in The Rivals, with 'allegory' put for 'alligator'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mrs Malaprop in Sheridan's The Rivals says 'allegory' for alligator, and her name gives the term for such a word misused.

clue.text: It gave a name to muslin

definitions.text: It gave a name to muslin

parts.words: It gave a name to muslin
parts.note: the fine cotton fabric is named after the city in Iraq where it was made

explanation.walkthrough: Muslin was named after the city in Iraq where it was first made.
explanation.definitionFit: The fine cotton fabric takes its name from this city in northern Iraq.

parts.note: bis is Latin for twice, used in music for a repeat
to hop is to jump

explanation.surface: An address to a nobleman followed by a double leap.
explanation.walkthrough: BIS is Latin for 'twice', a direction in music to repeat a passage.
explanation.definitionFit: A Church of England prelate is addressed as 'My Lord'.

parts.note: a heraldic bird with wings and legs splayed out names the posture of a body stretched wide

explanation.definitionFit: The heraldic eagle with wings and legs extended gives its name to a sprawling, fully stretched posture.

parts.note: a plain definition: showing regret or sorrow

explanation.definitionFit: Showing sorrow or regret is being mournful.

parts.note: a musical direction to grow gradually quieter

explanation.definitionFit: A musical direction to fade gradually means becoming steadily quieter.
